home.title: Learn About Your Body
home.subtitle: A safe space to learn about menstruation and puberty
home.description: Everyone goes through changes as they grow up. This app helps you understand these changes in a friendly, easy-to-understand way.

boys.title: For Boys
boys.subtitle: Understanding Menstruation
boys.intro: Learning about menstruation helps you understand and support the people in your life.
boys.whyLearnContent: Understanding menstruation helps you be a better friend, brother, and family member. It breaks down barriers and helps everyone feel more comfortable.
boys.whatIsContent: Menstruation, or having a period, is a natural monthly process that happens in the female body. It's a sign that the body is healthy and working normally.
boys.howToHelpContent: Be understanding, don't make jokes about periods, and be supportive if someone needs help or feels unwell.

basics.title: Understanding Menstruation: The Basics
basics.intro: Let's start with the simple facts about menstruation. It's a natural process that happens in healthy bodies.
basics.whatIsText: Menstruation (also called a period) is when blood and tissue from the uterus comes out through the vagina. This happens once a month for most people with female reproductive systems.
basics.whyHappensText: Every month, the body prepares for a possible pregnancy. The uterus creates a soft, cushiony lining. If pregnancy doesn't happen, this lining isn't needed, so the body sheds it. That's a period!
basics.fact3: The menstrual cycle is about 21-35 days long
basics.fact4: It's a sign of a healthy, functioning body
basics.fact5: About half the world's population experiences periods
basics.biologyText: The menstrual cycle is controlled by hormones. These are natural chemicals in the body that send messages. Think of them like the body's text messages telling different parts what to do!

whyMiss.title: Why Girls Might Miss School or Feel Unwell
whyMiss.intro: Understanding why someone might not feel their best during their period helps you be more supportive.
whyMiss.crampsDesc: Muscle contractions in the uterus can cause stomach pain, similar to a muscle cramp during exercise
whyMiss.tirednessDesc: Hormonal changes and losing blood can make someone feel more tired than usual
whyMiss.headachesDesc: Changes in hormone levels can trigger headaches or make someone feel dizzy
whyMiss.moodChangesDesc: Hormones affect emotions, so someone might feel more sensitive, irritable, or sad
whyMiss.backPainDesc: The cramping can extend to the lower back, making it uncomfortable to sit or stand
whyMiss.understandingText: These symptoms aren't an excuse or exaggeration. They're real physical experiences. Some people have mild symptoms, others have severe ones. Being understanding and not making jokes makes a huge difference.

support.title: How to Be a Supportive Friend
support.intro: You can make a real difference by being understanding and helpful. Here's how:
support.do1Desc: If a friend seems tired or uncomfortable, give them space without prying
support.do2Desc: Don't make a big deal out of it. It's a regular part of life for many people
support.do3Desc: If someone needs a sweater or asks you to carry something, help out without questions
support.do4Desc: If a school club or sports team asks you to keep supplies, say yes
support.do5Desc: If you hear someone making period jokes, let them know it's not okay
support.dont1Desc: Period jokes aren't funny. They make people feel embarrassed and ashamed
support.dont2Desc: Don't ask someone if they're on their period. It's private
support.dont3Desc: It's natural biology, like sweating or growing. Don't act disgusted
support.dont4Desc: If someone has an accident, keep it private. Don't tell others
support.scenario1: A classmate seems quieter than usual
support.scenario1Action: Give them space, but let them know you're there if they need anything
support.scenario2: Someone asks to borrow your jacket
support.scenario2Action: Lend it without asking why. They might need it for privacy
support.scenario3: A friend says they can't play sports today
support.scenario3Action: Accept it without pressing for details. Suggest something low-key instead.

myths.title: Busting Common Myths
myths.intro: There are many myths about periods that simply aren't true. Let's clear them up!
myths.fact1: Periods are completely natural and healthy. Menstrual blood is just blood and tissue, no different from a nosebleed
myths.myth2: Girls can't swim or exercise during periods
myths.fact2: Most people can do everything they normally do, including swimming, running, and playing sports. Exercise often helps reduce cramps!
myths.myth3: You can tell when someone has their period
myths.fact3: You cannot tell by looking at someone. Period products are designed to be discreet
myths.fact4: Most periods last 3-7 days. The average is about 5 days
myths.myth5: Only girls need to learn about periods
myths.fact5: Everyone benefits from understanding menstruation. It helps build supportive, educated communities
myths.fact6: Periods are a normal part of life. Open conversations help remove shame and stigma
myths.fact7: Period cramps are real and can be quite painful. They're caused by muscle contractions in the uterus
myths.myth8: You lose a lot of blood during a period
myths.fact8: The average period involves only about 2-3 tablespoons of blood. It might look like more because it's mixed with other fluids.

quiz.title: Test Your Knowledge
quiz.intro: Let's see what you've learned! Choose the best answer for each question.
quiz.q1b: The body shedding the uterine lining when pregnancy doesn't occur
quiz.q2: How long does a typical period last?
quiz.q3: What's the BEST way to support a friend during their period?
quiz.q3a: Ask them lots of questions about it
quiz.q3b: Tell everyone so they can help
quiz.q3c: Be understanding, patient, and don't make jokes
quiz.q3d: Pretend you don't know anything about periods
quiz.q4b: You can always tell when someone has their period
quiz.q4c: People can't exercise during their period
quiz.q4d: Periods are a natural, healthy process
quiz.q5: What should you do if someone has a period accident at school?
quiz.q5a: Tell all your friends about it
quiz.q5b: Make jokes to lighten the mood
quiz.q5c: Be discreet and offer to help (like lending a jacket)
quiz.excellent: Excellent! You really understand how to be supportive!
quiz.good: Good job! You're on the right track!
quiz.needsWork: Keep learning! Review the sections again.

summary.title: Key Takeaways
summary.point3: Never make jokes or tease about periods
summary.point5: Educate yourself to be a better ally.

girls.title: For Girls
girls.subtitle: Your Body, Your Journey
girls.intro: Your body is amazing! Let's learn about the changes happening and how to take care of yourself.
girls.whatToExpectContent: Periods usually start between ages 9-16. Everyone's body is different, and that's perfectly normal!
girls.yourCycleContent: A menstrual cycle is typically 21-35 days. The period itself usually lasts 3-7 days.
girls.takingCareContent: Learn about different period products, managing cramps, and when to talk to a doctor.
girls.feelingGoodContent: Tips for staying comfortable, eating well, and managing your emotions during your period.
girls.empowermentText: Millions of people experience periods every day. It's a natural, healthy part of growing up. You've got this!

understanding.title: Understanding Menstruation
understanding.whatIsUterusText: Your uterus is a special organ in your body, about the size of your fist. It's shaped like an upside-down pear and sits in your lower belly, between your bladder and your intestines. The uterus has thick, muscular walls and a soft inner lining. Every month, this lining gets thicker and richer with blood vessels, preparing to nurture a baby if pregnancy happens. Think of your uterus as an amazing, self-renewing organ that plays an important role in your body's monthly cycle. When you get your period, the uterus is simply shedding its lining and preparing to build a fresh one - it's your body's natural way of staying healthy!
understanding.whatIsText: Menstruation is a natural monthly process where the uterus sheds its lining through the vagina. This happens when pregnancy doesn't occur. It's a sign your body is working properly!
understanding.whyHappensText: Each month, your body prepares for a possible pregnancy by building a cushiony lining in the uterus. If pregnancy doesn't happen, your body doesn't need this lining, so it sheds it. That's your period!
understanding.howLongText: Most periods last 3-7 days, with an average of 5 days. Your cycle (from the start of one period to the start of the next) is usually 21-35 days.
understanding.firstPeriodText: Getting your first period can feel exciting and a little scary. It usually happens between ages 9-16. You might notice brown or red spotting in your underwear. This is completely normal!

bodyChanges.title: Your Changing Body
bodyChanges.subtitle: Learn about the changes happening in your body
bodyChanges.breastsDesc: Your breasts will begin to grow and develop. They may feel tender sometimes. This usually happens before your first period.
bodyChanges.hairDesc: You'll notice hair growing in new places like underarms and pubic area. This is completely normal and natural.
bodyChanges.skinDesc: Your skin might become oilier, and you may get acne. Washing your face regularly and staying hydrated can help.
bodyChanges.heightDesc: You'll grow taller quickly during puberty. You might notice your feet, hands, and arms growing first.
bodyChanges.hipsDesc: Your hips may widen and your body will develop curves. Everyone develops at their own pace.
bodyChanges.emotionsDesc: Hormones can affect your mood. You might feel more emotional or sensitive. This is normal and temporary.

products.title: Period Products Guide
products.intro: There are many options for managing your period. Choose what feels most comfortable for you!
products.padsDesc: Soft, absorbent pads that stick to your underwear. Great for beginners. Change every 4-6 hours.
products.padsHow: How to use: Remove the backing paper and stick to the center of your underwear. Wrap used pads in toilet paper before disposing.
products.clothPadsDesc: Reusable fabric pads that snap onto underwear. Eco-friendly and economical. Wash after each use.
products.clothPadsHow: How to use: Position the cloth pad in your underwear and snap the wings around the sides to secure it. After use, rinse in cold water to remove blood, then wash with regular laundry using detergent. Air dry or tumble dry on low heat. Store clean pads in a dry place.
products.tamponsDesc: Small, absorbent tubes inserted into the vagina. Good for swimming and sports. Change every 4-6 hours.
products.tamponsHow: How to use: Insert gently at an angle. If inserted correctly, you shouldn't feel it. Remove by pulling the string.
products.cupsDesc: Reusable silicone cups that collect blood. Can be worn up to 12 hours. Eco-friendly option.
products.cupsHow: How to use: Fold and insert. Empty, rinse, and reinsert every 12 hours or as needed.
products.underwearDesc: Special absorbent underwear. Washable and reusable. Great as backup protection.
products.underwearHow: How to use: Wear like regular underwear. Rinse and wash after use.
products.choosingText: Start with pads if you're new to periods. You can try other options when you feel comfortable. Many people use different products at different times.

painManagement.title: Managing Cramps and Discomfort
painManagement.intro: Period cramps are common, but there are ways to feel better!
painManagement.heatDesc: A heating pad or hot water bottle on your lower belly can really help relax muscles and reduce pain.
painManagement.exerciseDesc: Gentle activities like walking, yoga, or stretching can help reduce cramps and boost your mood.
painManagement.hydrationDesc: Drink plenty of water. It helps reduce bloating and can ease cramps.
painManagement.restDesc: Your body is working hard. Make sure you get enough sleep and rest when you need it.
painManagement.foodDesc: Eat nutritious foods rich in iron and vitamins. Avoid too much salt, sugar, or caffeine.
painManagement.medicineDesc: Over-the-counter pain relievers can help. Always check with an adult before taking any medication.
painManagement.whenToTalk: When to Talk to an Adult
painManagement.severe: Pain is very severe and stops you from daily activities
painManagement.heavy: Very heavy bleeding (soaking through pads in 1-2 hours)
painManagement.irregular: Very irregular cycles after having periods for 2+ years
painManagement.other: Any other concerns or questions you have.

tracking.title: Tracking Your Cycle
tracking.intro: Keeping track of your period helps you know when to expect it and understand your body better.
tracking.reason1: Predict when your next period will start
tracking.reason4: Share accurate information with healthcare providers
tracking.method1: Mark the first day of your period on a calendar
tracking.method2: Count the days until your next period starts
tracking.method3: Note any symptoms or changes you experience
tracking.method4: Look for patterns after tracking for a few months
tracking.calendarDesc: Click on the date your period started. Track for a few months to see your pattern.

myths.title: Period Myths vs Facts
myths.intro: Let's bust some common myths and learn the facts!
myths.myth1: You can't swim during your period
myths.fact1: You can absolutely swim! Use a tampon or menstrual cup, and you're good to go.
myths.fact2: Periods are completely natural and nothing to be ashamed of. It's a sign of a healthy body.
myths.myth3: You lose a lot of blood
myths.fact3: Most people lose only 2-3 tablespoons of blood during their entire period.
myths.fact4: Exercise is actually helpful! It can reduce cramps and improve your mood.
myths.fact5: Cycles vary! Anywhere from 21-35 days is normal. Your cycle is unique to you.
myths.myth6: You can't get pregnant during your period
myths.fact6: While unlikely, it's possible. This is why period education is important!
myths.fact7: Virginity is not a physical state. Using tampons doesn't change anything about your body.
myths.myth8: Period blood is different from regular blood
myths.fact8: Period blood is just like any other blood, mixed with tissue and fluids from the uterine lining.

empowermentSection.title: You're Amazing!
empowermentSection.message1: Your body is doing something incredible. Menstruation is a sign of health and strength.
empowermentSection.message2: Millions of people around the world experience periods every day. You're part of a global sisterhood!
empowermentSection.message3: It's okay to have questions, feel confused, or need help. That's what learning is all about.
empowermentSection.message4: Talk to trusted adults - parents, guardians, teachers, or healthcare providers. They're here to help you.
empowermentSection.message5: Remember: periods are natural, normal, and nothing to be embarrassed about!

quickTips.title: Quick Tips
quickTips.tip1: Keep a small kit with pads, wipes, and spare underwear in your bag
quickTips.tip2: Dark-colored clothes can help you feel more confident
quickTips.tip3: Set a reminder on your phone to change products regularly
quickTips.tip4: Keep a jacket or sweater tied around your waist just in case
quickTips.tip5: Tell a trusted friend or teacher so you have support at school.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Got questions? We've got answers!

questions.a1: A period (also called menstruation) is the monthly shedding of the uterine lining through the vagina. It's a completely natural and healthy part of the menstrual cycle. During each cycle, the body prepares for a possible pregnancy by thickening the uterine lining. When pregnancy doesn't occur, this lining is released. Most periods last 3-7 days, with an average of 5 days.
questions.q2: At what age do periods start?
questions.a2: Periods typically start between ages 9-16, with most girls getting their first period around 12-13 years old. However, everyone's body develops at its own pace, so there's a wide range of what's considered normal. If you haven't gotten your period by age 16, or if you have concerns, it's a good idea to talk to a healthcare provider.
questions.a3: The menstrual cycle is the monthly process your body goes through to prepare for a possible pregnancy. It typically lasts 21-35 days, with 28 days being average. The cycle has four phases: menstruation (your period), the follicular phase (when eggs develop), ovulation (when an egg is released), and the luteal phase (when the body prepares for pregnancy or the next period).
questions.q4: How much blood is lost during a period?
questions.a4: Most people lose about 2-3 tablespoons (30-40ml) of blood during their entire period, though it often seems like more. The blood mixes with other vaginal fluids, which can make it appear to be a larger amount. If you're soaking through a pad or tampon every hour for several hours, or passing large clots, talk to a healthcare provider.
questions.q5: What are period cramps and why do they happen?
questions.a5: Period cramps (dysmenorrhea) are caused by contractions of the uterus as it sheds its lining. The uterus is a muscle, and these contractions help push out menstrual blood. Prostaglandins, hormone-like substances, trigger these contractions and can also cause pain. Mild to moderate cramping is normal, but severe pain that interferes with daily life should be discussed with a doctor.
questions.q6: Is it normal to have irregular periods?
questions.a6: Yes, especially in the first 1-3 years after your period starts! It takes time for your body to establish a regular pattern. Irregular periods can also be caused by stress, changes in weight, intense exercise, illness, or hormonal changes. However, if your periods are very unpredictable after the first few years, or if you experience other concerning symptoms, consult a healthcare provider.
questions.a7: Absolutely! Stress can significantly impact your menstrual cycle. High stress levels can delay your period, make it lighter or heavier, or even cause you to skip a period entirely. This happens because stress hormones can interfere with the hormones that regulate your cycle. Managing stress through exercise, adequate sleep, and relaxation techniques can help maintain a more regular cycle.
questions.q8: What's the difference between spotting and a period?
questions.a8: Spotting is light bleeding that happens between periods—usually just a few drops that might appear pink or brown. A period is regular menstrual bleeding that's heavier and lasts several days. Spotting can happen for many reasons: ovulation, starting or stopping birth control, pregnancy, or hormonal changes. Occasional spotting is usually normal, but frequent spotting should be discussed with a healthcare provider.
questions.a9: There are several options: Pads (disposable or reusable cloth) stick to your underwear and absorb blood. Tampons are inserted into the vagina. Menstrual cups are reusable silicon cups that collect blood. Period underwear has built-in absorbent layers. Each has pros and cons—pads are easy for beginners, tampons and cups are good for swimming, and reusable options are eco-friendly. Try different products to find what works best for you.
questions.q10: How often should I change my pad or tampon?
questions.a10: Change pads every 4-6 hours, or sooner if they're saturated. Tampons should be changed every 4-6 hours and never left in longer than 8 hours to prevent toxic shock syndrome (TSS), a rare but serious condition. Even if flow is light, change tampons regularly. Menstrual cups can be worn for up to 12 hours before emptying. Always wash hands before and after changing any product.
questions.a11: TSS is a rare but serious bacterial infection that can be associated with tampon use, especially super-absorbent tampons left in too long. Symptoms include sudden high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, or a rash resembling sunburn. To prevent TSS, use the lowest absorbency tampon needed, change tampons regularly (every 4-6 hours), and never leave one in overnight without changing it. If you experience these symptoms while using tampons, remove the tampon immediately and seek medical help.
questions.q12: Can I use tampons if I'm a virgin?
questions.a12: Yes! Using tampons doesn't affect virginity. Virginity is a social concept, not a medical one, and is about sexual activity, not tampon use. The hymen (a thin tissue around the vaginal opening) is flexible and has an opening that allows menstrual blood to flow out. Tampons can pass through this opening. While the hymen might stretch, this doesn't define or affect virginity in any medical sense.
questions.q13: How do I choose the right pad or tampon size?
questions.a13: Choose based on your flow, which may vary throughout your period. Light days need regular or light products, heavy days need super or overnight products. For tampons, always use the lowest absorbency that works—don't use super tampons on light days. For pads, overnight or maxi pads work for heavy flow or nighttime, while regular or thin pads work for light to medium flow. You might use different sizes throughout your period.
questions.q14: Is it safe to swim during my period?
questions.a14: Yes, it's completely safe to swim during your period! Use a tampon or menstrual cup while swimming. The water pressure can temporarily slow or stop flow while you're in the water, but it's best to use protection. Pads won't work while swimming as they absorb water. Change into dry clothes and a fresh tampon or clean cup after swimming.
questions.q15: How should I dispose of pads and tampons?
questions.a15: Never flush pads or tampons down the toilet—they can cause plumbing problems. Wrap used products in toilet paper or the wrapper from your new product, then place in a trash bin. Many bathrooms have special disposal bins. At home, you can keep a small trash can with a lid in the bathroom. For discretion when disposing in public, you can carry small disposal bags.
questions.q16: How do I prevent leaks at night?
questions.a16: Use overnight or extra-long pads designed for sleeping, which have more coverage. Wear snug-fitting underwear to keep products in place. You might also wear dark-colored pajamas or place a towel on your bed. Some people use period underwear as backup protection. If you use tampons, insert a fresh one before bed, but remember to change it first thing in the morning (within 8 hours).
questions.q17: Is it normal to have blood clots during my period?
questions.a17: Small blood clots (smaller than a quarter) are completely normal during periods, especially on heavier flow days. They form when blood pools before leaving the body. However, if you're passing large clots (bigger than a quarter), having very heavy flow, or experiencing significant pain, talk to a healthcare provider as this could indicate a condition that needs treatment.
questions.q18: How can I track my period?
questions.a18: Mark the first day of your period on a calendar or use a period tracking app. Track the number of days your period lasts and count the days until your next period starts (this is your cycle length). After tracking for 2-3 months, you'll start to see patterns. Also note symptoms like cramps, mood changes, or flow heaviness—this information can be helpful when talking to healthcare providers.
questions.q19: Can I exercise during my period?
questions.a19: Absolutely! Exercise during your period is not only safe but can actually help reduce cramps and improve mood. Physical activity releases endorphins, natural pain relievers. Light exercise like walking, yoga, or swimming can be especially helpful. However, listen to your body—if you're experiencing severe cramps or feeling very fatigued, it's okay to rest or do gentler activities.
questions.q20: Can I go to school with my period?
questions.a20: Yes! Having your period shouldn't stop you from going to school or doing regular activities. Be prepared with supplies, know where school bathrooms are, and consider keeping an emergency kit in your locker. If you experience severe cramps or heavy bleeding that interferes with school, talk to a parent or school nurse about getting accommodations or seeing a doctor.
questions.q21: What if I get my period at school and don't have supplies?
questions.a21: Don't panic—this happens to everyone! Ask the school nurse, who almost always has supplies. You can also ask a female teacher or trusted friend. Many schools now have free products in bathrooms. In an emergency, fold toilet paper into a pad shape until you can get proper supplies. Consider keeping an emergency kit in your locker or backpack.
questions.q22: Can I play sports during my period?
questions.a22: Yes! Many professional athletes compete while on their periods. Use whatever period product feels most comfortable—tampons or menstrual cups are often preferred for sports. Wear comfortable, breathable athletic clothes, and consider dark-colored bottoms if you're worried about leaks. Exercise can actually help reduce cramps and boost your mood. Stay hydrated and listen to your body.
questions.q23: Why do I feel so tired during my period?
questions.a23: Period fatigue is common and caused by several factors: hormonal changes (especially drops in estrogen and progesterone), loss of iron through menstrual blood, interrupted sleep from cramps or bathroom trips, and your body working hard during menstruation. Combat fatigue by getting adequate sleep, eating iron-rich foods (leafy greens, lean meats, beans), staying hydrated, and doing light exercise.
questions.a24: PMS refers to physical and emotional symptoms that happen in the days or weeks before your period. Common symptoms include mood swings, irritability, sadness, bloating, breast tenderness, headaches, fatigue, and food cravings. PMS is caused by hormonal changes in your cycle. It typically goes away once your period starts. Regular exercise, adequate sleep, stress management, and a balanced diet can help manage symptoms.
questions.q25: Why do I get emotional or moody before my period?
questions.a25: Hormonal fluctuations before your period, particularly changes in estrogen and progesterone, affect neurotransmitters in your brain that regulate mood. These changes can make you feel more emotional, irritable, anxious, or sad. This is completely normal! Self-care strategies like exercise, adequate sleep, healthy eating, and stress management can help. If mood changes are severe or interfering with life, talk to a healthcare provider.
questions.q26: How can I manage period cravings?
questions.a26: Period cravings, especially for sweets or salty foods, are driven by hormonal changes. Instead of fighting them completely, make healthier choices: opt for dark chocolate instead of candy, fruit when craving sweets, nuts when craving salty snacks. Stay hydrated, eat balanced meals with protein and fiber to stabilize blood sugar, and allow yourself small portions of foods you crave. Don't feel guilty—some cravings are your body's way of signaling nutritional needs.
questions.q27: Is it normal for periods to smell?
questions.a27: A slight metallic smell (like iron) is normal because menstrual blood contains iron. However, strong or foul odors can indicate an infection or that a product has been left in too long. Prevent odors by changing products regularly (every 4-6 hours), washing daily with mild soap and water, and wearing breathable cotton underwear. If you notice a strong, unpleasant smell, especially with other symptoms, see a healthcare provider.
questions.q28: What are some myths about periods?
questions.a28: Common myths include: 'You can't swim during your period' (FALSE—you can!), 'Periods are dirty' (FALSE—it's natural and healthy), 'You lose a lot of blood' (FALSE—usually just 2-3 tablespoons), 'You can't exercise' (FALSE—exercise often helps!), 'All cycles are 28 days' (FALSE—21-35 days is normal), and 'You can tell when someone has their period' (FALSE—products are discreet). Understanding facts helps reduce stigma.
questions.q29: Can you get pregnant during your period?
questions.a29: While it's less likely, it is possible to get pregnant if you have sex during your period, especially if you have short cycles or long periods. Sperm can survive in the body for up to 5 days, so if you ovulate early, pregnancy could occur. This is why period education is important. If you're sexually active, understanding contraception and reproductive health is crucial.
questions.q30: When should I talk to a doctor about my period?
questions.a30: See a doctor if: periods are extremely painful and interfere with daily life, bleeding is very heavy (soaking through a pad/tampon every 1-2 hours), periods last longer than 7 days, you haven't started your period by age 16, cycles are shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days (after the first few years), you have severe PMS, periods suddenly stop for 3+ months (when not pregnant), or you have any other concerns.
questions.q31: What foods can help with period symptoms?
questions.a31: Iron-rich foods (spinach, red meat, beans, fortified cereals) help replace iron lost through bleeding. Foods with omega-3s (salmon, walnuts, flaxseeds) reduce inflammation and cramping. Calcium and vitamin D (dairy, fortified plant milks) may reduce PMS symptoms. Complex carbs (whole grains, vegetables) stabilize blood sugar and mood. Magnesium (bananas, dark chocolate, nuts) can reduce cramps. Stay hydrated and limit caffeine, salt, and sugar which can worsen symptoms.
questions.q32: Can periods stop due to exercise or weight?
questions.a32: Yes. Intense athletic training or very low body weight can cause periods to stop (amenorrhea). This happens because the body needs a certain amount of body fat and energy to maintain reproductive functions. While missing a period occasionally might not be harmful, long-term amenorrhea can lead to bone loss and other health issues. If your periods stop due to exercise or weight changes, consult a healthcare provider.
questions.q33: What's the difference between a pad and a liner?
questions.a33: Pads are thicker and designed to absorb menstrual flow. They come in various sizes for different flow levels. Panty liners are much thinner and smaller, designed for very light spotting, backup protection with tampons/cups, or discharge on non-period days. Liners aren't absorbent enough for menstrual flow—they're for light protection only. Always use a proper pad during your period.
questions.q34: Why is my period brown or dark red?
questions.a34: Period blood color varies and can be bright red, dark red, or brown. Brown blood is simply older blood that took longer to leave the body—it's oxidized, like how a cut turns brown as it heals. This is especially common at the beginning or end of your period when flow is lighter. Dark red blood is also normal, especially during heavy flow. Only be concerned if you notice gray tissue, very unusual colors, or symptoms like fever or odor.
questions.a35: Yes, but with precautions. Never leave a tampon in for more than 8 hours to reduce TSS risk. Insert a fresh tampon right before bed and change it immediately upon waking, even if it's only been 6-7 hours. For overnight, use the absorbency you need but no higher. Many people prefer pads overnight for longer, uninterrupted sleep and reduced TSS risk.
questions.q36: What should I keep in a period emergency kit?
questions.a36: A good emergency kit includes: 2-3 pads or tampons of varying absorbencies, panty liners, an extra pair of underwear, pain relief medication (with parent permission), personal wipes or small pack of tissues, a small plastic bag for disposal or soiled clothes, and hand sanitizer. Keep one kit in your backpack or locker and another at home. Consider adding a small snack and a heating pad if space allows.

anatomy.title: Interactive Anatomy Explorer
anatomy.subtitle: Tap any organ to learn what it does and how it changes through your cycle.
anatomy.tapPrompt: Tap an organ in the diagram — or select one below — to see what it does.
anatomy.svgAriaLabel: Illustrated diagram of the female reproductive system
anatomy.educationalNote: This diagram is educational and simplified. It is not a medical reference.

phaseOverview.menstrual: The uterus sheds its lining. This is your period — usually days 1–5. Hormone levels are low. You may feel cramping as the uterus contracts.
phaseOverview.follicular: After your period, oestrogen rises and the uterine lining starts rebuilding. In the ovaries, several follicles begin growing — one will become dominant.
phaseOverview.ovulation: A surge of LH hormone triggers the dominant follicle to release a mature egg. The egg travels toward the fallopian tube. This usually happens around day 14.
phaseOverview.luteal: After ovulation, the follicle becomes the corpus luteum and releases progesterone. The uterine lining thickens further, ready in case a fertilised egg arrives.

uterus.name: Uterus
uterus.what: A pear-shaped muscular organ in your lower abdomen. Its inner lining (the endometrium) builds up and sheds each month. If pregnancy happens, a fertilised egg implants here.

phases.menstrual: The lining sheds as your period — this is what the bleeding is. The uterus contracts gently to push the lining out.
phases.follicular: The lining starts to regrow and thicken, nourished by rising oestrogen levels.
phases.ovulation: The lining continues to build. The uterus is in a welcoming, receptive state.
phases.luteal: Progesterone makes the lining thick and spongy — ideal for a fertilised egg. If pregnancy doesn't happen, the lining will shed again.

leftOvary.name: Left Ovary
leftOvary.what: One of two almond-shaped organs that store eggs (ova) and produce hormones like oestrogen and progesterone. You are born with all the eggs you will ever have.

phases.menstrual: Resting. Hormone levels are at their lowest.
phases.follicular: Several follicles (tiny fluid-filled sacs each containing an egg) begin to grow here or in the right ovary.
phases.ovulation: If the dominant follicle developed here, it releases an egg this phase.
phases.luteal: If ovulation occurred here, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, producing progesterone.

rightOvary.name: Right Ovary
rightOvary.what: One of two almond-shaped organs that store eggs (ova) and produce hormones like oestrogen and progesterone. You are born with all the eggs you will ever have.

phases.menstrual: Resting. Hormone levels are at their lowest.
phases.follicular: One follicle becomes dominant and grows rapidly, producing increasing oestrogen.
phases.ovulation: The dominant follicle releases a mature egg — ovulation! The egg is swept into the nearby fallopian tube.
phases.luteal: The empty follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone until the next period begins.

fallopianTubes.name: Fallopian Tubes
fallopianTubes.what: Two slender tubes connecting each ovary to the uterus. Tiny hair-like cilia sweep the egg along toward the uterus. Fertilisation usually takes place here.

phases.menstrual: Quiet and at rest during this phase.
phases.follicular: The tube prepares to receive an egg — cilia activity increases.
phases.ovulation: The fringed end (fimbria) sweeps the released egg into the tube. The egg travels toward the uterus over 3–4 days.
phases.luteal: The tube continues to move the egg (or nothing, if unfertilised) toward the uterus.

cervix.name: Cervix
cervix.what: The lower narrow part of the uterus that connects to the vagina. It produces mucus that changes throughout the cycle. During childbirth it dilates to let the baby pass.

phases.menstrual: Slightly open to allow the lining to flow out. Mucus is minimal.
phases.follicular: Mucus becomes clearer and more fluid — like egg white — to help sperm travel if needed.
phases.ovulation: Mucus is at its clearest and most stretchy. The cervix is slightly softer and more open.
phases.luteal: Mucus thickens and becomes a barrier. The cervix firms up again.

vagina.name: Vagina
vagina.what: A muscular canal that connects the uterus to the outside of the body. Period blood, cervical mucus, and discharge exit through here. It also self-cleans through natural discharge.

phases.menstrual: The pathway for menstrual blood to leave the body. Some discharge mixing with blood is normal.
phases.follicular: Discharge may increase and become clear or white as oestrogen rises.
phases.ovulation: Discharge is often at its most noticeable — clear and slippery.
phases.luteal: Discharge may reduce or become thicker and creamier as progesterone rises.

teachers.title: For Teachers
teachers.subtitle: Guiding Students Through Puberty
teachers.intro: This guide helps teachers create a safe, supportive classroom environment where students can learn about menstruation with confidence and without stigma.
teachers.whyLearnContent: Teachers play a crucial role in shaping how students perceive menstruation. A well-informed teacher can reduce shame, prevent bullying, and ensure all students feel comfortable in school.
teachers.incorrect: Not quite. Review the sections and try again.

basics.title: Understanding Menstruation: What Teachers Need to Know
basics.intro: Before you can teach or support students, it helps to have a clear, factual understanding of what menstruation is and how it affects young people day to day.
basics.whatIsText: Menstruation (a 'period') is the monthly shedding of the uterine lining when pregnancy does not occur. It typically lasts 3–7 days and repeats every 21–35 days. It is a completely normal physiological process.
basics.whyMattersTitle: Why It Matters in the Classroom
basics.whyMattersText: Students who menstruate may experience physical discomfort, emotional changes, or anxiety about leaks and hygiene. Understanding this helps you respond with empathy rather than frustration or dismissal.
basics.keyFacts: Key Facts Every Teacher Should Know
basics.fact1: Menstruation usually begins between ages 9 and 16
basics.fact2: Cramps, fatigue, headaches, and mood changes are medically documented symptoms
basics.fact3: Some students experience severe pain (dysmenorrhoea) that is not 'exaggerated'
basics.fact4: Access to hygiene products during school hours is a real and common challenge
basics.fact5: Shame and stigma around periods can negatively affect attendance and academic performance
basics.biologyText: The menstrual cycle is regulated by hormones — primarily oestrogen and progesterone. These same hormones affect mood, energy, concentration, and sleep. A student who seems withdrawn or fatigued may simply be in a difficult phase of their cycle.

classroom.title: Creating a Safe & Inclusive Classroom
classroom.intro: The way teachers talk — and don't talk — about menstruation sends a powerful message to students. Here is how to build a classroom culture of respect.
classroom.do1Desc: Saying 'menstruation' and 'uterus' instead of euphemisms models that this is a normal topic, not something shameful
classroom.do2Desc: Implement a 'no questions asked' pass for hygiene needs. Requiring students to explain in public causes unnecessary embarrassment
classroom.do3Desc: Maintain a small, discreet supply of pads or tampons in the classroom or direct students to where they can get them
classroom.do4Desc: Treat period-related teasing the same as any other form of bullying. Make clear it is not acceptable
classroom.do5: Include boys and all students in the conversation
classroom.do5Desc: When educating the class about puberty, include everyone. Ignorance among boys often fuels stigma
classroom.dont1: Don't ask a student publicly if they are on their period
classroom.dont1Desc: This is an invasion of privacy and can cause significant embarrassment
classroom.dont2: Don't dismiss physical complaints as excuses
classroom.dont2Desc: Period pain is real. A student asking to rest or go to the nurse should be taken seriously
classroom.dont3Desc: Comments like 'it's just cramps' minimise genuine discomfort and discourage students from seeking help
classroom.dont4Desc: If a student has a leak or an accident, handle it privately and discreetly to preserve their dignity
classroom.scenario1: A student asks to leave class urgently
classroom.scenario1Action: Let them go without interrogation. A quick 'of course' is enough. Follow up privately if needed.
classroom.scenario2: You notice a student looks pale and uncomfortable
classroom.scenario2Action: Quietly check in. Offer them the option to go to the nurse or rest without drawing attention.
classroom.scenario3: Boys are making jokes about a classmate's period
classroom.scenario3Action: Address it firmly in the moment: 'That comment is not acceptable.' Follow up with a broader class conversation about respect.

supporting.title: Supporting Girls Through Their Period at School
supporting.intro: Practical strategies to help students who menstruate feel safe, comfortable, and able to focus on learning.
supporting.strategy1Desc: Allow students to move or adjust their position. Cramps can make sitting still extremely painful
supporting.strategy2Desc: A hot water bottle or even a warm drink can significantly reduce cramping. Keep this option available
supporting.strategy3Desc: If a student is visibly unwell, allow them to work quietly at their desk rather than participate in active tasks
supporting.strategy4Desc: Make it clear — through your actions — that students can come to you if they need support without fear of embarrassment
supporting.strategy5Desc: If a student regularly struggles on certain days each month, note it privately and plan accordingly
supporting.absenceNoteText: Some students miss school because of severe period symptoms. Rather than penalising attendance, explore whether flexible arrangements (catching up work, resting in school) can keep them engaged. Persistent absence due to periods can indicate an underlying condition like endometriosis — encourage parents to consult a doctor.

boys.title: Helping Boys Understand and Be Allies
boys.intro: Boys who understand menstruation are less likely to tease, more likely to offer support, and contribute to a healthier, more respectful school culture.
boys.whyText: Stigma around menstruation is largely driven by ignorance. When boys receive the same education as girls, it normalises the topic, reduces bullying, and prepares them to be supportive partners, brothers, and colleagues in the future.
boys.talkingPoints: Key Messages to Share with Boys
boys.point1: Menstruation is a normal, healthy biological process — not something dirty or shameful
boys.point2: Period symptoms are real. A classmate who is unwell is not making excuses
boys.point3: Period jokes are hurtful and are a form of bullying
boys.point4: Being a good friend means being discreet, patient, and non-judgmental
boys.point5: Helping a classmate in need — lending a jumper, carrying something — is a sign of maturity and kindness
boys.activity1: Run a mixed-group discussion about myths vs facts
boys.activity1Desc: Use anonymous question cards so boys can ask without embarrassment
boys.activity2Desc: Ask students to act out how they would respond if a friend was unwell at school
boys.activity3: Use this app's 'For Boys' section together
boys.activity3Desc: Walk through the content as a class to ensure all students receive the same baseline understanding

myths.title: Myths Teachers Should Address
myths.intro: These misconceptions circulate among students and can cause real harm. Be ready to address them confidently.
myths.myth1: Periods are impure or make a person unclean
myths.fact1: Menstruation is a healthy biological process. No cultural or religious interpretation should be used to shame or restrict a student
myths.myth2: Girls use periods as an excuse to avoid work
myths.fact2: Period symptoms — cramps, fatigue, nausea — are medically documented. A student experiencing them deserves the same consideration as one with a headache
myths.myth3: Boys don't need to learn about periods
myths.fact3: Educating all students reduces stigma, bullying, and ignorance. Boys benefit from this knowledge throughout their lives
myths.myth4: Talking about periods openly will embarrass students
myths.fact4: Students are more embarrassed by secrecy and shame than by clear, matter-of-fact education from a trusted adult
myths.fact5: Dysmenorrhoea (severe period pain) affects up to 20% of people who menstruate and can be debilitating. It is never 'just cramps'
myths.myth6: Students should just take painkillers and get on with it
myths.fact6: While painkillers can help, some students cannot take them. Offer a range of support options and flexibility
myths.fact7: Accidents happen. How a teacher responds defines how the rest of the class responds. Discretion and compassion are the appropriate reactions
myths.myth8: This topic is only relevant for a few students
myths.fact8: Roughly half your students will menstruate. All students will be in relationships with, work alongside, or care for people who do. This topic is universally relevant

quiz.title: Check Your Understanding
quiz.intro: A short quiz to check the key ideas from this guide. Choose the best answer for each question.
quiz.q1: A student rushes out of class without asking permission. You later find out she had a period emergency. What is the most appropriate response?
quiz.q1a: Reprimand her for leaving without permission
quiz.q1b: Check in privately, acknowledge the situation, and review your bathroom pass policy
quiz.q1c: Announce to the class that she had an emergency
quiz.q2: Boys in your class are laughing about a classmate 'being on her period'. What should you do?
quiz.q2a: Ignore it — boys will be boys
quiz.q2b: Quietly warn the boys after class
quiz.q2c: Address it immediately and firmly, then follow up with a conversation about respect
quiz.q2d: Send the laughing boys out of the room
quiz.q3: A student frequently misses school around the same time each month. What is the most likely explanation and best response?
quiz.q3a: She is skipping school and should be disciplined
quiz.q3b: She may have severe period symptoms; speak with her (and parents if needed) to explore support and encourage a doctor's visit
quiz.q3c: Nothing — attendance is not a teacher's concern
quiz.q3d: Tell her classmates so they can help
quiz.q4: Which of the following best describes your role when a student has a period accident in class?
quiz.q4a: Announce the situation so other students can help
quiz.q4b: Ignore it so the student isn't embarrassed
quiz.q4c: Handle it discreetly: quietly provide support, allow the student to change, and ensure the class moves on without attention being drawn to the incident
quiz.q4d: Document it as a safeguarding concern
quiz.q5: What is the single most effective thing a teacher can do to reduce period stigma in the classroom?
quiz.q5b: Only discuss it during dedicated health lessons
quiz.q5c: Model calm, matter-of-fact language and behaviour whenever the topic arises naturally
quiz.q5d: Leave period education entirely to parents
quiz.excellent: Excellent! You are well prepared to support your students.
quiz.good: Good work! Review the sections once more to reinforce your knowledge.
quiz.needsWork: Keep going! Re-read the guide and try again.

summary.title: Key Takeaways
summary.point1: Menstruation is a normal, healthy process — treat it as such
summary.point2: Your language and reaction set the tone for the entire class
summary.point3: Practical accommodations (passes, supplies, flexible seating) make a real difference
summary.point4: Educate all students — reducing ignorance reduces stigma
summary.point5: Persistent severe symptoms may indicate a medical condition — encourage professional support
